Summary: There is no better part of your life to take total control than your finances. So why be stupid? The easiest way to lose money is by being stupid. Just by being smart you can save you hundreds if not thousands of dollars a year.

Remember when you got your first job and you got your first paycheck and all you wanted to do is spend the money? For those of you who got your first big boy job out of college and got that first check that is larger than any check you had ever receieved, how you just wanted to go out and spend it?

We are programmed by advertisers, marketers, and the media to be a consumer. That means spending your money. In order to truly be smart financially, you have to deprogram yourself from those impulses. Here some easy, basic ways to be smart and not stupid with your money.

  1. Avoid all debt

    In my opinion the only debt that is OK is a 15 year fixed rate mortgage. All other debt(credit cards, student loans, car leases or loans) should be avoided at all costs. Student Loans may be trickier and trickier to avoid these days, but there is no excuse for credit cards or auto loans. I understand that you can get a credit card and pay off the balance right away to earn the rewards/points that come with that, and if you have the outright discipline to do that, great. But most people just can't be trusted with credit cards, so if you don't think you can exercise self-control, avoid them. Debt is the #1 way to bleed wealth and money. If you have debt, pay it off as soon as you can. The quicker you pay it off, the less you have to pay in interest in the long run. Pay off all debt before moving onto stocked emergency funds, investments, retirement plans, and mortgages.

  2. Don't spend money on shit you don't need.

    Do you really need a custom built stereo for your car? Do you really need to take a weekend vacation to Las Vegas? Do you really need another DVD for your DVD collection? Simply saying no to your impulses can save you a lot of money. If you budget well and have the allocated/budgetted income for things, go ahead. But ask yourself "Do I really need this?" One of my favorite quotes comes from Dave Ramsey: "People go broke because they are trying to impress people they don't like by spending money they don't have on things they don't need". Remember, just because you can buy something doesn't mean you can afford it. There is nothing wrong with taking a vacation or buying a new DVD or a fancy sound system, just make sure it fits within your short and long term budget and financial goals.

  3. It can wait

    The main reason so many people use debt and credit cards and spend money they don't have on things they don't have patience. We live in an instant gratification culture so people want things now. They want the new iPhone now. They want that new car NOW. They want that big TV NOW. Instead, learn patience and save up your money so you can buy it when you can afford it.

  4. Say no to drugs

    Drugs are a money pit with no upside and tons of downside. In the financial world you are told to avoid things that have no upside and tons of downside. Drugs are a money pit, plain and simple. Avoid at all costs.

  5. Buy Used Cars Only, With Cash

    Cars depreciate in value tremondously upon driving it off the lot. So why would you buy one new? Why would you finance or lease one? All ways to lose money. Always buy your cars used, with cash. Let other people buy them new and take the depreciation hit. Financing cars is a bad idea because its debt and you will end up paying way more than it is worth in the long run once interest is factored in. Leasing is an even worse idea, you have to bear all the risks and downside of ownership without actually owning it, and lease payments are calculated to rip you off. There is a reason why dealers push leases so hard, it is their cash cow. Buy cars used with cash. So what if that means you can't drive a BMW and have to buy a 10 year old beater instead. It's about the long run. Buy the beater with cash now so in the long run you will be able to buy BMWs with cash and financial peace of mind later. Live within your means.

  6. Budget and Track Every Penny You Earn and Spend

    Allocate every cent you are going to spend before you actually spend it. Myself, on the 31st of every month I make a 1-month, 3-month, and 12-month budget. I allocate all of my income and expenses on a long excel spreadsheet and assign every cent I earn and tell it where it will go. Make every cent you earn have a purpose. Don't just let it sit in your bank account or wallet without a plan. That's how you end up spending money on shit you don't need impulsively. By planning a detailed short, medium and long term budget, you know where you stand financially and what you can or can't afford in the short, medium, or long term.

  7. Emergency Funds

    At the very least, have $1,000 socked away for an emergency and do not touch it. There was a recent article about how most Americans could not scrounge up $1,000 for an emergency. Don't be that person. I'd say this is even more important than paying off all debt. Have the $1,000 emergency fund for peace of mind. If you have paid off all debt, create a second stocked emergency fund that has 6 months of living expenses.

  8. Cook Your Own Food

    There is nothing wrong with eating out every now and then. But if you truly want to be smart financially you only do it occassionally. Most of your food should be eaten at home. Eating out is expensive compared to cooking your own food. I work with people who eat out lunch every day and there is no way that is cheap. Think of all the money they could save by bringing their lunch every day instead. Restaurants are an easy way to be parted with your hard earned money. Buy groceries instead.

  9. Working 2+ jobs is awesome

    Ever since I graduated college I have worked 2 jobs even though I don't have to. I choose to. I figure while I am young, I might as well maximize my earning potential by working as many hours as I can. This helps you get ahead early and get a head start. If you work a 40 hour job, great, but why not work a second job for another 20 hours? What better things do you have to do? Sit around and watch TV or play video games? The car I used to drive died on me so I bought my most recent used car with cash solely via the income of a 2nd job. If I had no 2nd job, it would have been a lot more difficult to buy a car with cash. If you are young and able, working a 2nd job can be a difference maker early on, especially if you have debt you need to pay off.

  10. Take the phrase "I deserve it" or "I owe it to myself" out of your vocabulary.

    This is a way people will justify spending money they don't have on things they can't afford. "I work so hard, I owe it to myself!" or "I deserve to treat myself!". There is nothing wrong with taking a vacation, or buying a new video game, if you can afford it and if it fits into your budget. It's a lot like dieting. People will be dieting, but say "I deserve to treat myself" and eat foods that are not diet-friendly, and then they become fat. Money is the same way. Don't use self-pity and "rewarding yourself" as a justification to hamster up an excuse to spend money you don't have.

  11. It's a marathon, not a sprint

    Being smart with money is about looking at the big picture and looking at the long term. Your financial situation will not always be how it is today, for better or worse. If you are smart with your money and make good decisions, chances are things will be better off in the long run. But too many people lose sight of the big picture, only weigh the short term benefits instead of the long term consequences, and are irresponsible with their money. You might not be able to afford that boat today, but just stay the course, be responsible, and in 10 years you will be able to buy an even nicer boat, with cash. Think about a person who spends $4 every day on coffee Starbucks. That's $20 a week or $1,000 a year. How would you like to have an extra $1,000 at the end of the year? $4 might not seem like much in the short run, but look at the big picture and it adds up.

Conclusions

  • Don't spend money you don't have on shit you don't need to impress people you don't like.

  • Live within your means

  • Say no to debt and drugs. If you have debt, pay it off as soon as possible before doing anything else.

  • Do not buy new cars and do not finance or lease vehicles. Used & Cash only.

  • Be patient and control your impulses

  • Create short and long term budgets and stick to them

  • Assign a purpose for every cent you earn. If you don't the money will disappear

  • Have $1,000 sitting in an emergency fund for emergencies only. Do not touch otherwise.

  • Eat out as infrequent as possible. It's OK every now and then, but a vast majority of your eating should be done at home.

  • If you are young and able, consider working 2 jobs even if you don't need to

  • Don't use self pity as a means to justify a dumb financial decision

  • It's all about the long run.

An interesting aspect to the issue of technological unemployment that is often overlooked in discussions like this is that machines aren't simply becoming more capable, thus obsolescing human jobs. They are also becoming smaller, more flexible, lower in minimum necessary production volumes, and cheaper. And so the cost of initiating production becomes lower and more accessible, the scale of production needed to be competitive becomes smaller, and it becomes possible to produce more closer to the consumer, reducing transportation overhead and shifting the spectrum of trade toward commodities rather than goods. It's now possible to initiate more kinds of production out-of-pocket or with small personal loans than ever before. The number of kinds of goods that can't be produced competitively in the space of a 2-4 car garage is shrinking. And so, automation is obsolescing capital about as fast as it is obsolescing jobs and where companies were once outsourcing jobs to the developing world, they're now off-loading the ownership of the means of production itself as its amortization--the cost of capital--is now a drag on competitiveness. Production capacity is now a commodity in itself.

And so the evolution of production points toward its demassification, localization, and eventual integration into the built habitat as a kind of on-demand municipal utility.
